To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the Easter Island and Tikopian examples illustrate the importance of institutions in achieving sustainable resource use and population stability and (2) the model shows that investment in human-made (i.e., nonrenewable) capital can lead to unsustainable growth and overshoot.

the Easter Island and Tikopian cases are consistent with the hypothesis that human-made capital can be an effective means of reducing the impact of population growth on the environment, but that the Easter Island case also shows that human-made capital does nothing to prevent population overshoot-and-collapse.

the Easter Island and Tikopian societies provide two contrasting examples of the relationship between natural resources, institutions, population growth, economic activity, and the evolution of human-made capital.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of culture in shaping human behavior and institutions and their impact on resource use and economic growth.
the role of institutions and human-made capital in the sustainability of natural resource use.
understanding the relationship between human behavior, natural resource systems, population growth, institutional change, and sustainability.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Easter Island and Tikopias' experiences illustrate that human societies can evolve to either a stable equilibrium, or a non-sustainable equilibrium.

Easter Island is a classic example of a resource-based economy that collapsed because it failed to develop institutions to control population growth, whereas Tikopia is a classic example where institutions were developed that controlled population growth.
Easter Island and Tikopians are not the same.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

human societies can learn from nature and that the key to sustainable development is not only to understand the natural resource base and human-made capital stock, but also the social institutions governing the interaction of these two components of the economy.
Easter Island is a cautionary tale of the consequences of ignoring resource constraints.
the Easter Island story is a cautionary tale for the future of our own society, while the Tikopia example is one to be emulated in the future.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the sustainability of natural resource systems depends critically on institutional arrangements.
the Easter Island and Tikopian experiences are not isolated events, but rather, part of a larger pattern of resource depletion and collapse that has occurred repeatedly in preindustrial societies.
human-made capital and population size are endogenous variables, and the institutions that govern their relationship are key to sustainable development.
